title: Sweeps compliance
summary: Prize promotion law basics, official rules, marketing consent, data protection and platform policies for prize ads, plus the red flags that mean an offer should be skipped. You finish with a compliance file, monitoring thresholds and an incident routine for every offer you run.

lessons.title: Sweepstakes, contests and lotteries
objectives: By the end you can tell a sweepstakes, a contest and a lottery apart using three elements.
By the end you can explain 'no purchase necessary' and the free entry method.
By the end you know which questions to ask about prize promotion law in each geo you target.

steps.p: A legal sweepstakes and an illegal lottery can look identical in an ad. The difference is one element, usually whether people pay to enter. Get it wrong and the advertiser faces fines, the network drops the offer and every lead you sent goes unpaid. You need to recognise the line yourself.

d.b: One element separates a draw from a lottery
d.s: Learn the three elements before you promote any prize.

steps.say: Here's why this matters. A legal sweepstakes and an illegal lottery can look identical in an ad. The difference is one element, usually whether people pay to enter. Get it wrong, and the advertiser faces fines, the network drops the offer, and every lead you sent goes unpaid. So you need to recognise that line yourself, before you promote any prize.

steps.h: The three elements of a lottery
steps.p: In many countries, a promotion that has all three elements is a lottery. Private lotteries are usually illegal unless licensed. Remove any one element and it may become a lawful promotion.
steps.more: Consideration means something of value given to enter, usually a payment or a purchase. In some places it can also mean significant effort. A sweepstakes removes consideration: entry is free. A contest removes chance: winners are picked by skill, judged against stated criteria. This is the general pattern in the US, the UK and many other countries; the details differ, so check each geo.
d: Prize
Chance
Consideration
Lottery
steps.say: Look at the formula on screen. Prize, plus chance, plus consideration, equals a lottery. In many countries, a promotion with all three elements is a lottery, and private lotteries are usually illegal unless licensed. Consideration means something of value given to enter, usually a payment or purchase. Remove any one element and it may become lawful. A sweepstakes removes consideration, so entry is free. A contest removes chance, so winners are picked by skill. Details differ, so check each geo.

steps.p: Both are lawful in many places when run properly. As a sweeps affiliate you will mostly promote sweepstakes. Know the contest model too, because some offers mix them, for example 'answer a question to enter'.
steps.say: Compare the two columns. A sweepstakes is prize plus chance, with no payment to enter, a required free entry method, and a winner drawn at random. A contest is prize plus skill, a fee is allowed in some places, the judging criteria are published, and the winner is chosen on merit. Both are lawful in many places when run properly. As a sweeps affiliate you'll mostly promote sweepstakes, but some offers mix the two, like answer a question to enter.

steps.p: If buying something gives an entry, there must also be a free way to enter with the same chance of winning. This is often called the alternative method of entry, or AMOE. The rules must explain it clearly, not bury it.

d.b: Buying must never improve your chances
d.s: A free entry route with equal odds keeps the draw lawful in many geos.

steps.say: Here's a key rule: no purchase necessary. If buying something gives an entry, there must also be a free way to enter, with the same chance of winning. This is often called the alternative method of entry, or A M O E. The rules must explain it clearly, not bury it. Buying must never improve your chances.

steps.p: Payment is the obvious one. Watch for the hidden ones. If entrants have to pay or give up something of value to enter, the promotion may be a lottery in that geo.
d: Purchase|buying a product to enter
Entry fee|paying any amount
Premium SMS|a paid text to enter
Paid shipping|'free prize, pay postage'
Heavy effort|in some places, check locally
steps.say: Payment is the obvious kind of consideration. Watch for the hidden ones. Look at the cards. A purchase to enter. An entry fee of any amount. A premium S M S, meaning a paid text to enter. Paid shipping, the free prize where you pay postage. And in some places, heavy effort, so check locally. If entrants have to pay or give up something of value to enter, the promotion may be a lottery in that geo.

steps.p: Our understanding at the time of writing, for orientation only. Laws change and details matter, so treat every line as a question to confirm, not an answer. We are not certain this is current; check the regulator's own site or a local lawyer before relying on it.
steps.more: In the US, New York and Florida have long required registration and a bond when the total prize value of a game of chance is over $5,000. That threshold is our understanding, not legal advice. In South Africa, section 36 of the Consumer Protection Act sets rules for promotional competitions, including limits on what entrants can be charged. For Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana, we are not certain which regulator approves which kind of promotion today. Ask the network which approvals the sponsor holds, and confirm locally.

steps.p: Ask these questions in order for every offer. If any answer is 'not sure', ask the network in writing before you spend. Write the answers in your offer file.
d: Is there a prize?
Is the winner chosen by chance?
Does anyone pay or buy to enter?
Is there a free entry route with equal odds?
Is the geo allowed in the rules?
steps.say: Here's how to classify a promotion. Ask these questions in order, for every offer. Is there a prize? Is the winner chosen by chance? Does anyone pay or buy to enter? Is there a free entry route with equal odds? And is the geo allowed in the rules? If any answer is not sure, ask the network in writing before you spend. Write the answers in your offer file.

steps.h: Example: the cost of an unlawful draw
steps.p: Example: you send 2,000 DOIs at $2.50 in a month. The regulator stops the draw because entry needed a paid SMS. The advertiser refuses to pay and the network reverses the period.

lessons.title: Official rules: what must be there
objectives: By the end you can list the elements a complete set of official rules usually contains.
By the end you can audit a rules page against an ad and spot mismatches.
By the end you can explain prize value, odds and winner selection in plain words.

steps.p: Official rules are the sponsor's promise to every entrant. Your ad repeats part of that promise. If your ad says something the rules do not, you are making a claim nobody will honour, and that is a misleading ad in your account.

d.b: Your ad can only promise what the rules promise
d.s: Read the rules before you write a single headline.

steps.say: Here's why this matters. Official rules are the sponsor's promise to every entrant, and your ad repeats part of that promise. If your ad says something the rules don't, you're making a claim nobody will honour, and that's a misleading ad in your account. So your ad can only promise what the rules promise. Read the rules before you write a single headline.

steps.p: This list is common to well-run sweepstakes in many countries. Exact legal requirements vary, but a rules page missing several of these is a warning sign.
d: Sponsor's legal name and address
Eligibility: age, geo, exclusions
Entry period with start and end dates
How to enter, including the free route
Prize, its value and number of winners
How and when winners are chosen and told
steps.say: This list is common to well-run sweepstakes in many countries. The sponsor's legal name and address. Eligibility, meaning age, geo and exclusions. The entry period with start and end dates. How to enter, including the free route. The prize, its value and the number of winners. And how and when winners are chosen and told. Exact legal requirements vary, but a rules page missing several of these is a warning sign.

steps.h: More clauses and what to check
steps.p: Beyond the basics, look for these. ARV means approximate retail value, the stated worth of the prize. Odds in a random draw usually depend on the number of eligible entries.
steps.say: Beyond the basics, look for these clauses. A R V means approximate retail value, the stated worth of the prize, and it should be a clear number, not up to. The odds should be explained honestly. There should be a way to request the winner list, a link to the privacy policy, a note on what the winner agrees to for publicity, and the governing law, meaning which country's law applies.

steps.p: Example: one $500 prize and 200,000 eligible entries means odds of 1 in 200,000. Rules usually say 'odds depend on the number of eligible entries'. Your ad must never suggest the odds are better than they are.
d: 1 prize
200,000 entries
steps.say: Here's an example of odds in plain words. Follow the formula. One five hundred dollar prize, divided by two hundred thousand eligible entries, gives odds of one in two hundred thousand. Rules usually say odds depend on the number of eligible entries. Your ad must never suggest the odds are better than they are.

steps.p: A good rules page is readable on a phone. Headings, short clauses and the free entry route stated near the top. If you need a lawyer to find the prize value, the page is not doing its job.

page.h: June $500 gift card draw: official rules
page.p: Sponsor: Example Rewards Ltd. Entry 1-30 June. Free to enter online or by post. One prize, ARV $500. Winner drawn at random on 1 July and contacted by email.

steps.say: A good rules page is readable on a phone. Look at this one. It names the sponsor, gives the entry dates, one to thirty June, says it's free to enter online or by post, states one prize with an A R V of five hundred dollars, and explains the winner is drawn at random on the first of July and contacted by email. Headings, short clauses, and the free route near the top. If you need a lawyer to find the prize value, the page isn't doing its job.

steps.p: Open the rules page next to your planned ad. Go through it in this order and write a yes or no for each step. Any 'no' must be fixed by the sponsor before you run.

steps.title: Find the sponsor
steps.text: Look for a legal company name and address, not just a brand.

page.p: Example Rewards Ltd, registered address listed.

steps.title: Check eligibility
steps.text: Age and geo must match your targeting exactly.

steps.title: Find the free route
steps.text: The free entry method should be easy to follow and give equal odds.

steps.say: Let's audit a rules page. Open it next to your planned ad. Tap Next to follow each step, and write a yes or no for each. First, find the sponsor, a legal company name and address, not just a brand. Second, check eligibility, so age and geo match your targeting exactly. Third, find the free route, easy to follow with equal odds. Fourth, match the prize, value and winner count to your headline. Fifth, save a dated screenshot, because rules can change mid-campaign. Any no must be fixed by the sponsor.

steps.h: Ad vs rules: match or mismatch
steps.p: Most rules problems for affiliates are mismatches. The prize in the ad is bigger, more specific or more certain than the prize in the rules. Read your ad next to the rules, line by line.
steps.say: Most rules problems for affiliates are mismatches. Compare the columns. On the left, the ad says win a new iPhone, but the rules say a smartphone or three hundred dollars. The ad says ten winners daily, but the rules say one winner per month. On the right, the ad says enter to win a three hundred dollar prize, one winner, drawn the first of July, and the rules say the same. Read your ad next to the rules, line by line.

steps.h: Example: rules summary for your prelander
steps.p: A short summary under the entry button helps people understand the draw. Copy the facts from the rules, keep them short, and always link to the full rules. Never paraphrase in a way that changes the meaning.

d.text: No purchase necessary. Open to US residents 18+. Entry 1-30 June. One $500 gift card (ARV $500). Odds depend on eligible entries. Sponsor: Example Rewards Ltd. Full official rules: [link]
d.note: Example wording; take every fact from the real rules.

steps.say: A short summary under the entry button helps people understand the draw. The text on screen is example wording. It says no purchase necessary, who can enter, the entry dates, the prize and its value, that odds depend on eligible entries, the sponsor's name, and a link to the full official rules. Copy the facts from the real rules, keep them short, and always link to the full rules. Never paraphrase in a way that changes the meaning.

steps.h: Ask whether prizes are really awarded
steps.p: You cannot audit a draw yourself, but you can ask. A sponsor running a real draw answers easily. Vague answers or silence are a reason to pause. Example exchange below; save the reply in your file.

messages.text: Before I scale 3107: was the May prize awarded, and can entrants request the winners list as the rules say?
Example answer: yes, May winner was paid on 3 June. Winners list is available by email request, per section 9 of the rules.

In this example chat, the buyer asks the manager whether the May prize was awarded, and whether entrants can request the winners list as the rules say. The example answer: yes, the May winner was paid on the third of June, and the list is available by email request. A sponsor running a real draw answers easily. Vague answers or silence are a reason to pause. Save the reply in your file.

steps.p: Each of these turns a lawful offer into a misleading ad. They usually come from writing the ad first and checking the rules later, or never.
d: Bigger prize in the ad|copy the prize from the rules
'Daily winners' that are not|state the real number
Brand-name prize not in rules|use the rules' wording
Old rules snapshot|re-check rules each month
steps.say: Each of these mistakes turns a lawful offer into a misleading ad. Look at the cards. A bigger prize in the ad, so copy the prize from the rules. Daily winners that aren't, so state the real number. A brand-name prize that isn't in the rules, so use the rules' wording. And an old rules snapshot, so re-check the rules each month. They usually come from writing the ad first and checking the rules later, or never.

steps.p: The prize must actually be awarded, to a real winner chosen the way the rules say. Many rules also offer a winners list on request, which is a simple way to check the draw is real.

d.text: Never invent winners, show fake winner names or photos, or imply more winners than the rules state. If you cannot confirm prizes are awarded, do not promote the draw.

steps.say: The prize must actually be awarded, to a real winner, chosen the way the rules say. Many rules also offer a winners list on request, which is a simple way to check the draw is real. Read the warning: never invent winners, show fake winner names or photos, or imply more winners than the rules state. If you can't confirm prizes are awarded, don't promote the draw.

steps.p: Starting rules for every offer and every new ad. They take minutes and they are the evidence you will need if a platform or network ever questions your ads.
d: Do not run until all five audit steps are a yes
Re-audit when the entry period changes or each month
Any ad-to-rules mismatch: pause the ad, fix it, re-check
Keep a dated rules snapshot for every offer
steps.say: Here are starting decision rules for your rules audit. Don't run until all five audit steps are a yes. Re-audit when the entry period changes, or each month. For any mismatch between ad and rules, pause the ad, fix it and re-check. And keep a dated rules snapshot for every offer. These take minutes, and they're the evidence you'll need if a platform or network ever questions your ads.

takeaways: Your ad can only promise what the official rules promise.
Complete rules name the sponsor, eligibility, period, free entry, prize value and how winners are chosen.
Audit rules against every ad and keep a dated snapshot.

quiz.q: One prize, 50,000 eligible entries. What are the odds?
quiz.why: One prize divided among 50,000 entries is a 1 in 50,000 chance.

quiz.q: The rules offer 'a smartphone or $300 cash'. Which headline matches?
options: Enter to win a smartphone or $300
quiz.why: It repeats the prize as the rules state it, with no extra certainty or brand.

quiz.q: Which is missing from these rules: sponsor, eligibility, entry period, prize and ARV, winner selection?
quiz.why: Complete rules explain how to enter, including the free route.

Do not run it; never show unverified winners
quiz.why: Fake or unverified winners are misleading. Only real, permitted winner information may be shown.

quiz.q: The entry period changes mid-campaign. What does the starting rule say?
options: Re-audit the rules and update your snapshot
quiz.why: Re-audit whenever the entry period changes, and keep a dated snapshot.

lessons.title: Consent and data protection
objectives: By the end you can describe what valid marketing consent looks like on a form.
By the end you can name the main data protection and marketing laws for your key geos.
By the end you can show with numbers why honest consent earns more than tricked consent.

steps.p: In lead gen, consent is the product. A lead without clear consent cannot legally be marketed to in many geos, so the advertiser cannot use it, so it gets scrubbed. Tricked consent also creates complaints that damage the advertiser's email and SMS sending, which ends offers.

d.b: Consent is what the advertiser pays for
d.s: No clear consent, no usable lead.

steps.say: Here's why this matters. In lead gen, consent is the product. A lead without clear consent can't legally be marketed to in many geos, so the advertiser can't use it, and it gets scrubbed. Tricked consent also creates complaints that damage the advertiser's email and S M S sending, and that ends offers. No clear consent, no usable lead.

steps.p: Data protection laws in many countries describe consent in similar terms. Your form, or the advertiser's form you send people to, should meet all of these.
d: Freely given|not forced to enter
Specific|says what marketing and by whom
Informed|plain words, partners named
Unambiguous|an active tick or click
Recorded|time, source and wording kept
Withdrawable|easy to unsubscribe
steps.say: Data protection laws in many countries describe consent in similar terms. Look at the cards. Freely given, so nobody is forced. Specific, saying what marketing and by whom. Informed, in plain words, with partners named. Unambiguous, meaning an active tick or click. Recorded, with time, source and wording kept. And withdrawable, with an easy way to unsubscribe. Your form, or the advertiser's form you send people to, should meet all of these.

steps.p: The consent box is unticked. The text says who will contact the person, how, and how to stop. Partners are named behind a link. The button says what happens. This is the standard to look for in any offer you promote.

page.p: Email: ______  [ ] I agree that Example Rewards Ltd and the partners listed here may email me offers. Unsubscribe any time. Privacy policy.

steps.say: Here's an honest entry form on a phone. Notice the consent box is unticked. The text says who will contact the person, Example Rewards and the listed partners, how, by email, and how to stop, unsubscribe any time. Partners are named behind a link, and there's a privacy policy. The button says exactly what happens: enter the draw. This is the standard to look for in any offer you promote.

steps.p: The left column is common in low-quality funnels. It raises the form rate a little and destroys the lead's value. The right column is what advertisers who last actually want.
steps.say: Compare the two columns. Tricked consent uses a pre-ticked marketing box, hides consent in the rules, mentions partners with no list, and has a button that says see prize. Real consent uses an unticked box the person ticks, puts consent next to the button, links a named partner list, and the button says enter the draw. The left column raises the form rate a little and destroys the lead's value.

steps.p: Example figures, same 1,000 clicks, $1.20 SOI. The pre-ticked form converts more, but the advertiser scrubs leads with weak consent and complaints. The honest form wins on EPC.
steps.more: Example: 220 × 60% = 132 paid × $1.20 = $158.40. 190 × 88% = 167 paid × $1.20 = $200.40. The exact figures will differ on your offers. The direction is what matters: consent quality shows up in scrubs, and scrubs show up in EPC.
steps.say: Here's an example with the same thousand clicks and a one dollar twenty S O I, that's single opt-in, payout. Look at the table. The pre-ticked form gets two hundred and twenty leads, but only sixty percent are accepted, so a hundred and fifty eight dollars forty. The honest form gets a hundred and ninety, with eighty eight percent accepted, so two hundred dollars forty. The honest form wins on E P C, earnings per click. Your figures will differ, but consent quality shows up in scrubs.

steps.p: The main data protection and marketing laws for common geos. Our summary at the time of writing, not legal advice. Each has a regulator with guidance on its website; read it before collecting data there.
steps.more: Some highlights. POPIA in South Africa generally requires opt-in consent for direct marketing by electronic communication to people who are not existing customers. CAN-SPAM in the US is mainly an opt-out law for email: honest headers and subject lines, a physical address and a working unsubscribe. The TCPA is stricter for marketing calls and texts using automated systems and generally needs prior express written consent. Rules change; confirm with each regulator.
steps.say: Here are the main data protection and marketing laws for common geos, our summary at the time of writing, not legal advice. Nigeria has the Data Protection Act twenty twenty three, with the N D P C. Kenya, the Data Protection Act twenty nineteen, with the O D P C. South Africa, POPIA, with the Information Regulator. Ghana, the Data Protection Act twenty twelve. The E U and U K have G D P R. The U S has CAN-SPAM for email and the T C P A for calls and texts. Read each regulator's guidance first.

steps.p: In 2023 the US FCC adopted a 'one-to-one consent' rule for lead generators selling phone leads. Our understanding is that a US court struck it down in early 2025.

d.text: We are not certain of its current status. Check the FCC's site or a US lawyer before running any US offer that leads to calls or texts.

steps.say: Here's an area of real uncertainty. In twenty twenty three, the U S F C C adopted a one-to-one consent rule for lead generators selling phone leads. lessons.title: Platform policies for prize ads
objectives: By the end you can name the policy areas prize ads most often break.
By the end you can rewrite a rejected prize ad into an approvable, honest one.
By the end you can follow written rules after a rejection without trying to slip past review.

steps.p: Prize ads sit close to several policy lines: misleading claims, fake interface elements, personal attributes and data collection. One rejection is normal. A pattern of them can restrict your ad account, which stops every campaign you run, not only the sweeps one.

d.b: One bad prize ad can cost the whole account
d.s: Write ads that pass because they are honest, not because they are clever.

steps.say: Here's why this matters. Prize ads sit close to several policy lines: misleading claims, fake interface elements, personal attributes and data collection. One rejection is normal. A pattern of them can restrict your ad account, which stops every campaign you run, not only the sweeps one. So write ads that pass because they're honest, not because they're clever.

steps.h: Policy areas prize ads break most
steps.p: These areas appear in most big platforms' ad policies under different names, and prize ads touch almost all of them. Names and rules change; check Meta's current Advertising Standards and Help Center.

Fake interface|fake buttons, alerts, play icons
Personal attributes|'You, Ada, are selected'
Data collection|lead forms need a privacy policy

steps.say: These policy areas appear in most big platforms' ad policies, under different names, and prize ads touch almost all of them. Look at the cards. Misleading claims, like you won, fake odds or fake urgency. Fake interface, like fake buttons, alerts or play icons. Personal attributes, like naming the viewer as selected. Data collection, where lead forms need a privacy policy. Trademarks, meaning brand prizes without permission. And guaranteed outcomes. Names change, so check Meta's current Advertising Standards and Help Center.

steps.h: Example: the lie does not even win
steps.p: Example per 100,000 impressions. The misleading ad doubles the click rate, but accepted leads collapse because people feel tricked. Once you pay for the extra clicks, honest earns more, before you even count the account risk.

Only $13 more, and it also pays for twice the clicks if you buy on CPC, gets reported, and risks the account. On a CPC basis at $0.15: honest profit $40.32, misleading $233.28 − $360 = −$126.72.

lessons.title: Hidden charges, CC submits and red flags
objectives: By the end you can recognise funnels that lead to hidden charges or subscriptions.
By the end you can work out why a high CC-submit payout is often worth less than it looks.
By the end you can audit a full funnel on your phone before sending traffic.

steps.p: Some 'sweeps' funnels are not really about a prize. The prize is bait for a card number or a paid SMS subscription. They pay big, they hurt real people, and regulators in several countries have acted against affiliates who promoted them, not only advertisers.

d.b: If the prize is bait for a charge, walk away
d.s: A big payout is often the first red flag.

steps.say: Here's why this matters. Some sweeps funnels aren't really about a prize. The prize is bait for a card number, or a paid S M S subscription. They pay big, they hurt real people, and regulators in several countries have acted against affiliates who promoted them, not only advertisers. If the prize is bait for a charge, walk away. A big payout is often the first red flag.

steps.h: How a hidden-charge trap usually works
steps.p: This is the pattern to recognise. Each step looks small. Together they turn a 'free prize' into a monthly charge the person never clearly agreed to.
d: 'Free' prize ad
Card asked for 'shipping'
Small trial charge
Auto-renew in fine print
Monthly charge
steps.say: This is the pattern to recognise. Follow the flow. A free prize ad. Then a card is asked for, for shipping. Then a small trial charge. Then auto-renew hidden in the fine print. And finally, a monthly charge. Each step looks small. Together, they turn a free prize into a monthly charge the person never clearly agreed to.

steps.p: Any one of these is a reason to stop and ask questions. Two or more and you should skip the offer. They are often called dark patterns: design that pushes people into choices they would not make knowingly.
d: Card for a 'free' prize|why does free need a card?
Pre-ticked paid upgrade|consent by default
Premium SMS entry|cost hidden in small print
Fake countdown|false urgency
Price below the fold|hidden on purpose
No cancel route|hard to stop
steps.say: Here are the red flags in a funnel. Look at the cards. A card for a free prize, so ask why free needs a card. A pre-ticked paid upgrade, which is consent by default. Premium S M S entry, with the cost hidden in small print. A fake countdown, creating false urgency. A price below the fold, hidden on purpose. And no cancel route. These are often called dark patterns. One is a reason to ask questions. Two or more, skip the offer.

steps.p: Bad example, do not copy. The page calls the prize free, then asks for a card for postage. The subscription terms sit below the button in small text. A real person would not expect a monthly charge from this page.

page.p: Just pay $4.95 shipping. Card number: ______. (Small print: includes 14-day trial, then $89 a month.)

steps.say: This is a bad example, so don't copy it. The page says your free prize is waiting, then asks you to pay four ninety five for shipping, with a card number box. The subscription terms sit in small print: a fourteen day trial, then eighty nine dollars a month. A real person wouldn't expect a monthly charge from this page. Spot how the button just says claim now.

steps.p: Example: a CC-submit offer pays $35. Then 30% of sales charge back or refund and are clawed back. Your effective payout is $24.50 before the account reviews, payment processor problems and legal exposure.
steps.more: Example only. The real cost is larger. When chargebacks pile up, payment processors stop the advertiser, the offer dies mid-month and the network may not pay the period. Your ad account collects complaints and negative feedback. Meanwhile real people pay for something they did not knowingly buy. The maths looks good only until the first audit.
d: $35 payout
(1 − 30% clawbacks)
steps.say: Here's an example of the high payout trap. A C C submit offer pays thirty five dollars. Then thirty percent of sales charge back or refund and are clawed back. Follow the formula: thirty five dollars, times one minus thirty percent, gives twenty four fifty. And that's before account reviews, payment processor problems and legal exposure. Meanwhile, real people pay for something they didn't knowingly buy. The maths only looks good until the first audit.

steps.p: Example: the $35 CC-submit payout shrinks at every stage. After 30% clawbacks it is $24.50. If the processor stops the offer halfway through the month and the period is not paid, the average falls to about $12.25.
d: Advertised payout
After 30% clawbacks
Half the month unpaid
steps.say: Here's that same example as bars. Watch the payout shrink at every stage. The advertised payout is thirty five dollars. After thirty percent clawbacks, it's twenty four fifty. And if the processor stops the offer halfway through the month and that period isn't paid, the average falls to about twelve dollars twenty five.

steps.p: Our summary at the time of writing, not legal advice. All of these generally require clear terms, real consent before charging and fair treatment. We are not certain this is current; check the regulator's own site or a local lawyer before relying on it.
steps.more: ROSCA, the US Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act, generally requires clear disclosure of terms before taking billing details, express informed consent before charging, and a simple way to stop recurring charges. The FTC also made a broader 'click-to-cancel' rule in 2024; our understanding is that a US court set it aside in 2025. We are not certain of its current status; check before relying on it.
steps.say: Here's a summary of consumer laws that apply, at the time of writing, not legal advice. In the U S, the F T C Act and ROSCA, which covers online subscriptions. In Nigeria, the F C C P A twenty eighteen. In Kenya, the Consumer Protection Act twenty twelve. In South Africa, the Consumer Protection Act two thousand and eight. And in the U K, consumer protection and subscription rules. All of these generally require clear terms, real consent before charging and fair treatment. Check the regulator's own site before relying on this.

quiz.q: A paid upgrade box is pre-ticked below the entry button. What does the starting rule say?
quiz.why: Pre-ticked paid upgrades are consent by default, which is on the skip list.

lessons.say_intro: This lesson is about hidden charges, C C submits, that's credit card submit offers, and red flags. You'll learn to recognise funnels that lead to hidden charges, why a high payout is often worth less than it looks, and how to audit a full funnel on your phone.
lessons.say_outro: If a free prize is bait for a card number or paid S M S, walk away, because clawbacks shrink the payout and you can be liable too. Audit every funnel yourself. Your task: walk your offer's full funnel from your tracking link on your phone, without entering card details, screenshot each page, watch your inbox for forty eight hours, and note any red flags. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Your compliance file and monitoring rules
objectives: By the end you can build a compliance file for every offer you run.
By the end you can monitor complaint, unsubscribe and scrub signals with written thresholds.
By the end you know what to do, in order, when a network or regulator raises a problem.

steps.p: Sooner or later a network, platform or advertiser will ask you to prove something: what your ad said, what the rules said, where a lead came from. With a file you answer in minutes and keep your payouts. Without one you lose the argument by default.

d.b: If it is not written down, it did not happen

steps.say: Here's why this matters. Sooner or later, a network, platform or advertiser will ask you to prove something: what your ad said, what the rules said, where a lead came from. With a file, you answer in minutes and keep your payouts. Without one, you lose the argument by default. If it's not written down, it didn't happen. Your file is your defence.

steps.h: What goes in each offer's file
steps.p: One folder per offer. It takes about ten minutes to start and a few minutes a week to keep current. Date every item, because the question is always what was live on a given day.
d: Offer terms and payment terms, in writing
Dated official rules snapshot
Funnel audit screenshots
Every ad, with dates live and approvals
Consent wording and partner list
Network messages about compliance
steps.say: Keep one folder per offer. Here's what goes in it. Offer terms and payment terms, in writing. A dated official rules snapshot. Funnel audit screenshots. Every ad, with the dates it was live and its approvals. The consent wording and partner list. And network messages about compliance. It takes about ten minutes to start, and a few minutes a week to keep current. Date every item, because the question is always what was live on a given day.

steps.p: Keep a log sheet next to the folder. One row per change: new ad, rules change, rejection, network message. The pulsing table is the part you will be asked for most.
steps.say: Keep a log sheet next to the folder, with one row per change: a new ad, a rules change, a rejection, a network message. In this example log, look at the pulsing table. The first of June, a rules snapshot. The second, the funnel audit passed. The fifth, ad version two approved. Each row has its proof file. That table is the part you'll be asked for most.

steps.h: Signals to monitor and starting thresholds
steps.p: Starting thresholds to adapt. Ask the network or advertiser for complaint and unsubscribe rates by your sub ID; many will share them. Mailbox providers publish their own spam-rate guidance, which changes.
steps.more: The 0.1% and 0.3% spam figures come from large mailbox providers' published guidance for bulk senders, at the time of writing. We are not certain they are current; check Google's and Yahoo's sender guidelines. They apply to the advertiser's sending, but your traffic drives them, which is why advertisers watch complaints by source.
steps.say: Here are signals to monitor, with starting thresholds to adapt. Look at the table. Spam complaint rate, watched by sub I D, pause at point three percent, and aim for under point one. Scrub rate by sub I D, pause at two times your average. Ad rejections, pause at two on one offer. And negative comments that claim scam or charged. Ask the network for complaint and unsubscribe rates by your sub I D. The spam figures come from mailbox provider guidance, which changes.

steps.h: Example: when complaints cross the line
steps.p: Example: the advertiser emails 12,000 leads from your sub ID and gets 42 spam complaints. 42 ÷ 12,000 = 0.35%. That is above the 0.3% pause line. Pause that sub ID and look at the promise in its ads.
d: 42 complaints
12,000 emails
steps.say: Here's an example of complaints crossing the line. The advertiser emails twelve thousand leads from your sub I D, and gets forty two spam complaints. Follow the formula: forty two divided by twelve thousand is point three five percent. That's above the point three percent pause line. So you pause that sub I D, and look at the promise in its ads.

steps.p: Example message. This is how compliance problems usually arrive: politely, with a deadline. Your answer comes from your file. Reply fast, with facts and a fix, never with excuses.

messages.text: Hi, sub ID fb_as03 on offer 3107 shows a 0.35% complaint rate this week. Please send the ads used and pause if needed.
Paused fb_as03 now. Ads and approval dates attached from my log. Ad v1 implied urgency; replaced with v2 from the rules. Can you confirm when to resume?

steps.say: This example shows how compliance problems usually arrive: politely, with a deadline. The network says one sub I D shows a point three five percent complaint rate, and asks for the ads used. Notice the reply. The buyer has already paused the source, attaches the ads and approval dates from the log, names the cause, an ad that implied urgency, explains it was replaced with a version written from the rules, and asks when to resume. Fast, factual, with a fix.

steps.p: When any network, platform or advertiser raises a problem, follow these steps in this order. Speed and honesty protect your payouts more than any argument does.
d: Pause the source
Pull the file
Find the cause
Fix and document
Reply with facts
Resume only on approval
steps.say: When any network, platform or advertiser raises a problem, follow these steps in order. Pause the source. Pull the file. Find the cause. Fix it and document it. Reply with facts. And resume only on approval. Speed and honesty protect your payouts more than any argument does.

steps.p: Keep this reply template in your file. Fill it from your log. Short, factual and specific replies get sources resumed faster than long explanations, and they show the network you run a tidy operation.

d.text:
Sub ID: [id]  Offer: [id]
Paused at: [date, time]
Cause found: [what the ad or funnel said]
Fix: [new ad version, date approved]
Proof attached: [files from log]
Request: written approval to resume
d.note: Example template; adapt to your network.

steps.say: Keep this reply template in your file. The text on screen has slots for the sub I D and offer, when you paused, the cause you found, the fix with the new ad version and approval date, the proof attached from your log, and a request for written approval to resume. Fill it from your log. Short, specific replies get sources resumed faster than long explanations, and they show the network you run a tidy operation.

steps.p: A short note from the founder on why the boring paperwork matters as much as the ads, and why the best months are rarely the ones with the cheapest leads.
steps.d: My best months were never the ones with the cheapest leads. They were the ones where nothing came back to bite me.
steps.say: Here's a short note from Dchessking on why the boring paperwork matters as much as the ads. Here's the quote: My best months were never the ones with the cheapest leads. They were the ones where nothing came back to bite me.

steps.p: Each of these feels like saving time on the day. Each one costs far more later, when a payout is held and you cannot prove what you ran or when you ran it.
d: No dates on screenshots|date every file
Deleting old ads|keep them, paused
Arguing before pausing|pause first, then discuss
Verbal agreements|ask for it in writing
steps.say: Each of these mistakes feels like saving time on the day. Look at the cards. No dates on screenshots, so date every file. Deleting old ads, so keep them, paused. Arguing before pausing, so pause first, then discuss. And verbal agreements, so ask for everything in writing. Each one costs far more later, when a payout is held and you can't prove what you ran, or when.

steps.h: Compliance: you may hold personal data
steps.p: If you host forms or store leads, you may be a data controller under laws like Nigeria's NDPA, Kenya's DPA or POPIA. Some laws require registration with the regulator.

d.text: Keep only the data you need, secure it, delete it on schedule, and check whether you must register. We are not certain of every registration threshold; check the regulator.

steps.say: If you host forms or store leads, you may be a data controller under laws like Nigeria's N D P A, Kenya's D P A or POPIA, and some laws require registration with the regulator. Read the warning: keep only the data you need, secure it, delete it on schedule, and check whether you must register. We're not certain of every registration threshold, so check with the regulator.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt with your network. Check them weekly at a fixed time, and immediately whenever any message arrives about quality or compliance, even if your CPL looks healthy that week.
d: Complaint rate ≥ 0.3% on a sub ID: pause it
Scrub ≥ 2 × average on 50+ leads: pause it
Two ad rejections on an offer: stop the offer
Any regulator or network warning: pause first, reply within 24 hours
Resume only after written approval
steps.say: Here are starting rules for monitoring. A complaint rate of point three percent or more on a sub I D, pause it. A scrub of two times average or more, on fifty plus leads, pause it. Two ad rejections on an offer, stop the offer. Any regulator or network warning, pause first, and reply within twenty four hours. Resume only after written approval. Check these weekly at a fixed time, and immediately when any quality message arrives, even if your C P L, cost per lead, looks healthy.

takeaways: Keep one dated file and log per offer: terms, rules, funnel audit, ads, consent, messages.
Monitor complaints, scrubs, rejections and comments against written pause lines.
On any warning: pause, pull the file, fix, reply with facts, resume only on approval.
lessons.action: Create the compliance folder and log sheet for your chosen offer. Add the rules snapshot, funnel audit and offer terms you collected in earlier lessons, each with a date.

glossary.def: A dated folder of proof for one offer: terms, rules, audits, ads and messages.
Spam reports divided by emails delivered, often tracked by traffic source.
Any warning or problem raised by a network, platform, advertiser or regulator.
A written threshold at which you stop a source until it is fixed.

quiz.q: An advertiser sends 20,000 emails to your leads and gets 50 spam complaints. What is the rate and action?
quiz.why: 50 ÷ 20,000 = 0.25%. Below the 0.3% pause line but well above the 0.1% aim, so watch closely and review the ads.

quiz.q: A network flags a sub ID for complaints. What is the first step?
quiz.why: Pause first. Then pull the file, find the cause and reply with facts.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in an offer's compliance file?
quiz.why: Dated rules show what the promotion promised when your ads ran.

quiz.q: You host entry forms and store emails. What may you be under data protection law?
options: Only a processor with no duties
quiz.why: If you decide why and how personal data is used, you are likely a controller with duties.

quiz.q: When do you resume a paused source after an incident?
options: After written approval from the network
quiz.why: Resume only on written approval, and log it.

lessons.say_intro: In this final lesson, you'll build a compliance file for every offer, set written thresholds for complaints, unsubscribes and scrubs, and learn what to do, in order, when a network or regulator raises a problem.
lessons.say_outro: Keep a dated file and log for every offer, watch complaints, scrubs and rejections against written thresholds, and when a problem arrives, pause first, then reply with facts. Your task: create the compliance folder and log sheet for your chosen offer, and add the rules snapshot, funnel audit and offer terms you collected earlier, each with a date. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: An offer gives one entry per purchase and also lets people enter free by post with the same odds. What is it?
options: A sweepstakes with a free entry route
exam.why: A free alternative method with equal odds removes consideration in many geos.

exam.q: You want to send Kenyan traffic to a draw whose rules say 'US residents only'. What do you do?
options: Run it with a small budget
Ask the advertiser to edit the rules for you
Do not send Kenyan traffic to it
exam.why: Never target a geo the rules exclude.

exam.q: Rules: '1 winner, smartphone or $300'. Your ad: 'Win the new iPhone, 10 winners this week'. What is wrong?
options: Prize, brand and winner count all mismatch the rules
exam.why: Your ad can only promise what the rules promise: prize, value and number of winners.

exam.q: Pre-ticked form: 300 leads, 55% accepted. Honest form: 250 leads, 90% accepted. Payout $1.00. Which earns more and by how much?
You plan US traffic to an offer that leads to marketing texts, and you are unsure about current FCC consent rules. What do you do?
options: Run it; email rules cover it
Check current FCC guidance or a US lawyer and confirm written consent wording first
exam.why: Texts and calls are tightly regulated in the US and the rules have been changing.

exam.q: Your prize ad is rejected for misleading claims. Your colleague suggests writing 'w0n' instead of 'won'. What do you do?
options: Use an image of the word instead
Refuse: it is circumvention; rewrite from the rules
Move it to a new account
exam.why: Disguising claims to dodge review is circumvention and can end your access.

exam.q: A $38 CC-submit offer has 35% clawbacks and asks for card details for a 'free' prize. What do you do?
options: Skip it: card for a 'free' prize is on the skip list
exam.why: It is a red-flag funnel regardless of payout. Effective payout would be $24.70 before other risks.

exam.q: An advertiser reports 36 spam complaints from 10,000 emails on your sub ID. What do you do?
options: Pause the sub ID: 0.36% is above the 0.3% line
Ask for the complaints to be removed

exam.q: A network messages you about a complaint spike on Friday night. In what order do you act?
options: Pause, pull the file, find the cause, fix, reply, resume on approval
exam.why: Pause first and reply within 24 hours with facts from your file.

exam.q: Which statement about uncertain rules is right?
options: If a blog says it, it is current
If you are unsure, assume it is allowed
Rules only matter for big affiliates
If you are unsure whether a rule is current, check the regulator or platform before relying on it
exam.why: Laws and policies change. Check the source before you spend.
